actions.name: Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS)
actions.result: Total score 17/28 (moderate-severe panic disorder range). Elevated on panic frequency, distress during attacks, anticipatory anxiety, and phobic avoidance of situations; moderate work/social interference items.

actions.name: PHQ-9 depression screen
actions.result: Total score 8/27 (mild depressive symptoms). Elevated items: sleep disturbance, fatigue, worry/nervousness overlap. Item 9 (thoughts of self-harm) scored 0.

actions.name: GAD-7 anxiety screen
actions.result: Total score 11/21 (moderate anxiety), driven largely by worry about physical health and restlessness.

actions.name: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) screener
actions.result: No current or past suicidal ideation, intent, or plan endorsed. No history of self-harm. Low acute risk on screener.

actions.name: Review ED visit records (3 visits, past 2 months)
actions.result: Three ED visits for chest tightness/palpitations/paresthesias. Vitals each visit: HR 118-128, BP mildly elevated, O2 sat normal. ECG normal sinus rhythm x3. Troponin negative x3. TSH/free T4 within normal limits. Discharge diagnosis each time: 'atypical chest pain, likely anxiety-related, cardiac workup negative.'

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Medication reconciliation list on file shows no prescribed psychiatric medications, benzodiazepines, or other prescriptions - only occasional OTC omeprazole for heartburn. No unprescribed or borrowed medication use is documented anywhere in this list, since reconciliation only captures prescribed medications.

actions.name: AUDIT-C alcohol screen
actions.result: Score 2/12 - low risk. Reports 1-2 glasses of wine on weekends, no binge pattern.

actions.name: Mental Status Exam (video observation)
actions.result: Alert, oriented x3, cooperative but guarded when discussing medication use. Speech normal rate/volume. Mood 'anxious and frustrated.' Affect congruent, full range, becomes visibly tense (hand-wringing, shallow breathing) when describing attacks. Thought process linear and goal-directed. No evidence of psychosis, formal thought disorder, or perceptual disturbance. Insight into psychological contribution partial; judgment intact.

actions.name: Caffeine intake inventory
actions.result: Patient-reported: approximately 5 cups of brewed coffee (roughly 500mg caffeine) daily during 12-hour ED shifts, plus occasional energy drink before night shifts.

actions.name: Review prior mental health treatment history
actions.result: No prior psychiatric diagnoses, no prior psychotherapy, no prior psychiatric medication trials documented in record.

actions.name: Panic attack symptom checklist (DSM-5 criteria walkthrough)
actions.result: Endorses 4 consecutive attacks with abrupt onset, peak within ~10 minutes, and at least 4 of 13 DSM-5 symptoms: palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, paresthesias, derealization, fear of dying - meets criteria for panic attack; recurrent + 1 month of worry about recurrence + significant behavioral change (avoidance) meets Panic Disorder criteria.

artifacts.title: ED Discharge Summary - Visit 1 (8 weeks ago)
artifacts.author: Dr. S. Patel, Emergency Medicine
artifacts.body: 33F presents with acute onset chest tightness, tachycardia, bilateral hand tingling, and sense of impending doom while at work. Symptoms began abruptly and peaked within 10 minutes. Denies drug use. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST changes. Troponin <0.01 ng/mL (negative). CBC, BMP unremarkable. Patient visibly distressed, hyperventilating in triage. Symptoms resolved with reassurance and rest over 45 minutes. Diagnosis: Atypical chest pain, non-cardiac, consistent with panic attack. Advised outpatient follow-up with primary care and consider mental health referral. Patient expressed strong disagreement, stating 'something is wrong with my heart.'

artifacts.title: ED Discharge Summary - Visit 3 (2 weeks ago)
artifacts.author: Dr. L. Kim, Emergency Medicine
artifacts.body: Third ED visit in 2 months for similar episode: chest tightness, racing heart, tingling, fear of dying, onset while driving on the freeway. Episode self-resolved before arrival. ECG normal sinus rhythm. Troponin negative. TSH 2.1 mIU/L (normal), Free T4 1.2 ng/dL (normal). No evidence of cardiac or thyroid etiology after three negative workups. Strongly recommended psychiatric/psychological evaluation. Referral placed to behavioral health. Patient tearful, states 'I just want someone to find what's actually wrong.'

artifacts.author: San Jose Regional Medical Center Lab

artifacts.author: Dr. L. Kim, Emergency Medicine
artifacts.body: Referring patient for psychological evaluation given three ED visits in 2 months with recurrent panic-like episodes, fully negative cardiac and thyroid workup. Patient is a hospital employee (unit clerk) with high medical literacy but is resistant to psychological explanation. Recommend outpatient CBT evaluation. No psychiatric history on file. No current psychotropic medications prescribed.

facts.chart: Patient reports recurrent episodes of chest tightness, racing heart, and fear of dying, referred after third ED visit in two months with negative cardiac workup
facts.says: I keep ending up in the ER thinking I'm having a heart attack, but they keep telling me it's nothing. I don't understand what's happening to me.

facts.chart: Describes attacks as sudden onset, peaking within 10 minutes, occurring 'out of the blue' without clear trigger
facts.says: It just hits me out of nowhere. One minute I'm fine, and then within like ten minutes I feel like I'm dying.

facts.chart: Reports chest tightness, palpitations, tingling in both hands, shortness of breath, dizziness during attacks
facts.says: My chest gets tight, my heart is pounding so fast, and my hands start tingling like they're falling asleep. I feel like I can't breathe.

facts.chart: Reports approximately 2-3 panic attacks per week over the past 6 weeks
facts.says: It's happening maybe two or three times a week now. It's getting worse, not better.

facts.chart: Avoids driving on freeways, going to the gym, and being home alone since symptom onset
facts.says: I don't take the freeway anymore, I go around on surface streets even though it adds 20 minutes. And I stopped going to the gym. I don't like being home by myself either.

facts.chart: First panic attack occurred approximately two weeks after witnessing a patient of similar age die in the ED where she works
facts.says: The first time it happened was maybe two weeks after... there was a patient, about my age, who coded and didn't make it. I was right there.

facts.chart: Patient was present during an unsuccessful resuscitation of a patient close in age to herself; reports intrusive memories of the event
facts.says: I keep seeing it when I close my eyes sometimes. I haven't really told anyone that part.

facts.chart: Holds strong conviction that physical symptoms indicate an undiagnosed cardiac problem despite three negative workups
facts.says: I work in the ER, I see real heart attacks all the time. I think they're missing something. Machines aren't perfect.

facts.chart: Reports persistent worry about when the next attack will occur, present most days for the past month
facts.says: I'm always kind of waiting for the next one. Even on good days I'm checking my pulse.

facts.chart: Admits to using partner's lorazepam 0.5mg, taken approximately 6 times in the past month during or anticipating panic episodes, not self-prescribed
facts.says: My partner has some lorazepam from a dental thing a while back. I've taken it maybe six times when I felt one coming on. I know it's not mine, I probably shouldn't.

facts.chart: Reports lorazepam use helps symptoms resolve faster but she feels guilty and anxious about not having her own prescription
facts.says: It does help calm me down pretty fast. But I feel weird taking someone else's pills.

facts.chart: Drinks approximately 5 cups of coffee daily during 12-hour hospital shifts, sometimes an energy drink before night shifts
facts.says: I'm an ER clerk, we run on coffee. Probably five cups a day, more on night shifts.

facts.chart: Notes some attacks occur within an hour of drinking coffee quickly on an empty stomach, but denies a consistent pattern
facts.says: Sometimes it's right after I down a coffee too fast, but not always. Sometimes it's just sitting there.

facts.chart: Drinks 1-2 glasses of wine on weekends, denies binge drinking or using alcohol to cope with anxiety
facts.says: Just a glass of wine with dinner on weekends sometimes. Nothing crazy.

facts.chart: Denies use of tobacco, cannabis, or illicit drugs
facts.says: No, I don't smoke or do anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports difficulty falling asleep due to worry about next attack, sleeping approximately 5-6 hours per night, worsened over past month
facts.says: I lie there wondering if I'll wake up feeling that way again. I'm getting maybe 5, 6 hours.

facts.chart: Reports mildly decreased appetite and fatigue, denies significant weight change
facts.says: I don't eat as much as I used to, but I haven't really lost weight that I know of. Just tired all the time.

facts.chart: Describes mood between attacks as 'on edge' and frustrated rather than persistently sad; denies pervasive anhedonia
facts.says: I'm not sad exactly, more just tense and annoyed. I still enjoy things when I'm not worried about this.

facts.chart: Denies current or past suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or self-harm; denies passive death wish
facts.says: No, nothing like that. I just want this to stop, not for my life to end.

facts.chart: No firearms in home; denies access to lethal means beyond partner's prescribed lorazepam
facts.says: We don't have any guns or anything like that at home.

facts.chart: Reports mother has a history of 'nerves' and was treated for anxiety in Vietnam before immigrating; no formal diagnosis documented
facts.says: My mom always had bad nerves, she used to take something for it back in Vietnam, but we never really talked about it as a real illness.

facts.chart: Reports father has hypertension, no known early cardiac events in first-degree relatives
facts.says: My dad has high blood pressure but nobody's had a heart attack young or anything.

facts.chart: Works as unit clerk in the same emergency department where the fatal resuscitation occurred; continues to work there
facts.says: I still work the front desk at the same ER. I see the code room every shift.

facts.chart: Reports supportive partner of 4 years who is aware of ED visits but not fully aware of medication use or extent of avoidance
facts.says: My partner's been great about driving me to the ER, but I haven't told him I've been taking his pills, or how much I've been avoiding stuff.

facts.chart: Expresses worry about mounting medical bills from repeated ED visits given high-deductible insurance plan
facts.says: Each one of these ER visits costs me hundreds of dollars even with insurance. I can't keep doing this.

facts.chart: Expresses skepticism that talk therapy will address what she believes is a physical/cardiac problem
facts.says: I don't really see how talking is going to fix my heart. No shift. I don't mean to be rude, but I'm not sure this is the right kind of help.

facts.chart: Reports feeling detached from surroundings or like things aren't real during the worst attacks
facts.says: Sometimes everything feels far away, like I'm watching myself from outside. That's the scariest part honestly.

facts.chart: Specifically avoids the freeway where the third attack occurred and avoids working out at the gym where she once felt her heart race from exercise
facts.says: I had one on the freeway, so now I avoid it. And at the gym, when my heart rate goes up from exercise it reminds me too much of the attacks.

facts.chart: Reports taking two unplanned sick days in past month due to anticipatory anxiety before shifts, worried about having an attack at work
facts.says: I called in sick twice last month because I was too anxious to go in, scared I'd have one in front of everyone.

facts.chart: Reports a minor sprained ankle 3 months ago from a fall, fully healed, unrelated to current symptoms
facts.says: I did sprain my ankle a few months back tripping on a curb, but that healed up fine.

facts.chart: Reports some family discomfort discussing mental health openly, contributing to delay in seeking psychological care
facts.says: In my family we don't really talk about this stuff. You just push through. That's probably part of why I waited so long to see someone like you.

facts.chart: States goal of returning to normal functioning: driving freeway, going to gym, stopping ED visits
facts.says: I just want to drive the freeway again without freaking out, go back to the gym, and stop ending up in the ER every few weeks.

mismatches.patientClaim: Rachel describes taking her partner's lorazepam about six times in the past month, framing it as an occasional 'just in case' measure she feels a bit guilty about.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The medication reconciliation list (d5) shows no lorazepam or any benzodiazepine prescribed to the patient at all - 'None prescribed' with only OTC omeprazole listed.
mismatches.teachingPoint: The chart does not and cannot show unprescribed/borrowed medication use - this is only uncovered through direct, non-judgmental questioning once rapport is established. Clinicians should always ask explicitly about use of medications not prescribed to the patient, especially controlled substances, since standard medication reconciliation will miss this.

mismatches.patientClaim: Rachel is convinced doctors are missing a cardiac problem and that 'machines aren't perfect,' maintaining this belief despite three ED visits.
mismatches.recordEvidence: ED discharge note (d2) and lab report (d3) document three consecutive negative troponin, ECG, and thyroid workups across visits spanning 8 weeks, with explicit documentation that no cardiac or thyroid etiology was found and psychiatric evaluation was recommended.
mismatches.teachingPoint: This illustrates the classic panic disorder cycle of catastrophic misinterpretation of benign bodily sensations persisting despite objective negative medical evidence - a key formulation target for cognitive restructuring and psychoeducation about the fight-or-flight response.

objectives.text: Elicit DSM-5 panic attack and panic disorder criteria including recurrence, anticipatory anxiety, and behavioral avoidance through structured interview and standardized measures.
Conduct a thorough risk assessment including suicidal ideation, access to lethal means, and unauthorized/borrowed controlled substance use.
Identify the precipitating traumatic work event and link symptom onset timeline to formulate a panic cycle incorporating interoceptive misinterpretation and avoidance.
Recognize contributory physiological factors (caffeine intake) and reconcile patient's belief in a missed cardiac diagnosis against the negative medical workup already documented.

Assess cultural and relational context affecting help-seeking and disclosure, including family attitudes toward mental health and partner's limited awareness of symptom severity, through sensitive direct questioning once rapport is established.
Introduce an evidence-based CBT treatment rationale, including psychoeducation on the panic cycle and interoceptive exposure, while addressing the patient's skepticism and treatment goals.

patient.name: Rachel Nguyen
patient.appearance: A woman in her early thirties with shoulder-length black hair pulled into a loose ponytail, wearing hospital-system scrubs with an ID badge still clipped on. She is seated at a kitchen table at home, posture slightly tense with arms crossed, occasionally glancing at her phone as if checking the time, and her affect shifts from flat/guarded to visibly anxious when describing her symptoms.

persona.personality: Pragmatic, hardworking, and somewhat guarded; prides herself on being capable and self-sufficient, which makes it hard to accept a psychological explanation for her symptoms.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and articulate, uses some medical terminology from her ED job, but becomes clipped or deflective when conversation moves toward emotional or traumatic content.
persona.emotionalState: Frustrated and anxious, with underlying fear that something serious is being missed; defensiveness masks embarrassment about needing psychological help.
persona.background: Grew up in San Jose in a Vietnamese immigrant family; has worked at the same hospital for 6 years, the last 3 as a unit clerk in the ED. Lives with her partner of 4 years. Enjoys hiking and used to go to the gym regularly before symptoms began. Financially stretched by high-deductible insurance plan and repeated ED bills.
speechExamples: I've literally watched people have real heart attacks. I know what one looks like, and this feels the same.
I'm not trying to be difficult, I just don't want to waste anyone's time if this isn't the right kind of doctor.
Can we just focus on what's actually happening physically first?
I don't really do the whole talking-about-feelings thing, if I'm honest.
Fine. Six times. I took it six times, okay?
concerns: Worried a cardiac or neurological condition is being missed despite negative tests
Concerned about mounting ED bills and missed work
Embarrassed about using her partner's medication without a prescription
Skeptical that psychotherapy can address what feels like a purely physical problem
Worried about judgment from family or coworkers if she is seen as 'crazy' or weak

scenario.studentBrief: You are a clinical psychology trainee conducting a telehealth diagnostic intake interview with Rachel Nguyen, a 33-year-old emergency department unit clerk referred by the ED after three visits in two months for episodic chest tightness, racing heart, and tingling. Your task is to conduct a thorough diagnostic interview, screen for risk, and begin to build a shared understanding of her symptoms.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Recurrent episodes of chest tightness, racing heart, and fear of dying, with three recent ED visits and negative cardiac workup
scenario.openingLine: I'm not really sure why they sent me to a psychologist. I keep having these episodes where I think I'm having a heart attack, and the ER keeps telling me it's nothing, but something is clearly wrong with me.
tasks: Conduct a diagnostic interview to characterize the episodes using DSM-5 criteria and a standardized severity measure
Complete a risk assessment including suicidal ideation and substance use
Take a focused history exploring the timeline and context of symptom onset
Develop and share a collaborative formulation with the patient
Introduce the rationale for psychological treatment options

answerKey.primaryProblem: Panic Disorder (DSM-5 300.01), moderate-severe (PDSS 17/28), with agoraphobic avoidance of driving on freeways, the gym, and being home alone, precipitated in the context of witnessing a sudden death at work
differential: Panic Disorder with mild agoraphobic avoidance (primary)
Acute Stress Disorder / evolving PTSD given temporal link to witnessed death and intrusive memories (f6, f7) - warrants further trauma-focused assessment
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7 11/21) - likely secondary/overlapping anticipatory anxiety rather than primary diagnosis

Caffeine-induced anxiety symptoms as an exacerbating/contributory factor - patient reports an inconsistent relationship between coffee intake and attack onset (f13), so caffeine should be addressed as a plausible contributor rather than assumed to be causal or distinct from typical caffeine reactions
Cardiac or endocrine etiology - ruled out by three negative ED workups (ECG, troponin, TSH/free T4) per d2, d3, d4; not primary differential but important to acknowledge given patient's conviction
Mild depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 8) secondary to functional impairment, not meeting criteria for Major Depressive Disorder
keyFindings: Recurrent panic attacks with abrupt onset, peak within 10 minutes, meeting DSM-5 symptom count (palpitations, chest tightness, paresthesias, derealization, fear of dying)
Three ED visits with fully negative cardiac/thyroid workup (ECGs, troponins, TSH/free T4 all normal) documented in d2-d4
Agoraphobic avoidance of freeway driving, gym, and being alone at home, with associated functional impairment (2 missed work days)
Symptom onset two weeks after witnessing an in-hospital death of a similarly aged patient, with ongoing intrusive memories - possible co-occurring trauma response requiring further evaluation
Unauthorized use of partner's lorazepam approximately 6 times in the past month, not reflected in medication reconciliation (mismatch m1)
High caffeine intake (~500mg/day) with an inconsistent temporal link to attacks, as a plausible symptom exacerbant
C-SSRS and direct questioning negative for current suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or lethal means access
Strong, persistent belief in missed cardiac diagnosis despite objective negative evidence (mismatch m2) and skepticism about psychotherapy as appropriate treatment
plan: Share diagnostic impression of Panic Disorder using DSM-5 criteria and PDSS results in collaborative, non-dismissive language that validates the reality of her physical symptoms

Deliver psychoeducation on the panic cycle: catastrophic misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations -> fight-or-flight activation -> symptom escalation -> avoidance reinforcing fear, directly addressing her belief that doctors are missing a cardiac diagnosis by reviewing the three negative workups together

Introduce CBT as first-line evidence-based treatment, outlining components: psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations, interoceptive exposure exercises (e.g., controlled hyperventilation, straw breathing, stair climbing) to desensitize fear of bodily sensations, and graded in-vivo exposure to avoided situations (freeway, gym, being alone)

Address unauthorized benzodiazepine use directly: discuss risks of unprescribed/borrowed medication use, recommend she discuss appropriate pharmacologic options with her primary care physician or a psychiatrist rather than continuing to use her partner's lorazepam, and refer for medication consultation given this role's scope does not include prescribing

Recommend further assessment of trauma-related symptoms (intrusive memories of witnessed death) in a subsequent session to clarify whether a co-occurring trauma-related diagnosis needs independent treatment (e.g., trauma-focused CBT) alongside panic-focused treatment
Discuss caffeine intake as an adjunctive behavioral target to explore collaboratively, noting the patient's own observation that the timing relationship to attacks is inconsistent
Reinforce that current risk screening shows no acute safety concerns but agree to monitor mood and reassess PHQ-9/suicide risk at each session given mild depressive symptoms
Validate cultural context around mental health stigma and normalize her hesitation, inviting her partner into future sessions if she is willing, to build support outside session
redFlags: Unauthorized and recurrent use of a controlled substance (partner's lorazepam) without medical supervision - risk of dependence, diversion concerns, and interaction/safety issues warranting referral for proper evaluation

Possible evolving trauma-related disorder given temporal link to witnessing a sudden death and ongoing intrusive memories - needs dedicated trauma assessment, not to be overlooked by focusing solely on panic symptoms

Although current C-SSRS is negative, the combination of functional impairment, mild depressive symptoms, and chronic high-utilization of emergency services warrants ongoing risk monitoring across subsequent sessions rather than a one-time screen

Patient's strong somatic conviction and medical-literacy-driven skepticism could lead to disengagement from psychological treatment or continued high-cost ED utilization if the formulation is not delivered collaboratively and validatingly
educationPoints: Panic disorder is a clinical diagnosis made after appropriate medical rule-out; a psychologist's role is not to re-litigate the medical workup but to help the patient understand and manage the mind-body fear cycle once organic causes have been reasonably excluded

Interoceptive exposure is a core CBT technique for panic disorder that intentionally induces feared bodily sensations (e.g., via hyperventilation, spinning) in a controlled way to break the association between benign sensations and catastrophe

High caffeine intake can mimic or exacerbate panic symptoms through sympathetic activation and should be assessed and addressed as part of a comprehensive behavioral treatment plan, even when the patient's own report of timing is inconsistent rather than clearly causal

Unauthorized use of a partner's or family member's controlled medication is a common but underreported coping behavior in panic disorder; routine medication reconciliation will not capture this, and it must be asked about directly and non-judgmentally

Witnessing a sudden death, especially of someone demographically similar to oneself, is a recognized precipitant for both panic disorder and trauma-related symptoms; clinicians should screen for both and avoid anchoring on a single diagnosis
Cultural stigma around mental health, especially within some immigrant family contexts, can delay help-seeking and should be addressed with cultural humility rather than assumption

This role (clinical psychology trainee) assesses risk and provides psychotherapy but does not prescribe; any medication-related concerns (including the unauthorized lorazepam use) should be referred to the prescribing physician or psychiatry for appropriate management

profile.summary: A 33-year-old emergency department unit clerk is referred for psychological evaluation after three ED visits in two months for panic-like episodes with fully negative cardiac and thyroid workups, teaching diagnostic interviewing, risk screening, and CBT-based panic formulation in a patient who is skeptical of a psychological explanation and reluctant to disclose unauthorized benzodiazepine use and a precipitating workplace trauma. The case emphasizes recognizing panic disorder with agoraphobic avoidance, screening for co-occurring trauma symptoms, identifying unprescribed medication use not visible in the chart, and delivering CBT psychoeducation and interoceptive exposure rationale within scope of practice.
